scenes.title: AWS Glue: Table Definitions and ETL
scenes.narration: AWS Glue is a managed data integration service, and this overview shows how its two major roles work together. On the left are data sources such as S3 objects, database tables, and application data. The first orange step is discovery and cataloging. A Glue Crawler can inspect supported sources and create or update metadata in the Glue Data Catalog. That catalog describes tables, schemas, and partitions; it is not necessarily a copy of all your data. The second stage manages ETL jobs, which extract, transform, and load datasets into a form suitable for analytics or machine learning. Notice the options for on-demand, scheduled, and event-driven execution. The output column on the right shows analytics and AI consumers that benefit from prepared data. When answering an AWS architecture question, distinguish the catalog's metadata from the ETL job's processing work. The catalog helps applications discover and query a dataset, while the ETL logic actually changes or moves records. In a GenAI pipeline, this can prepare searchable enterprise data or analytics features before they reach retrieval or training workflows.

scenes.title: What AWS Glue Does
scenes.narration: Let's break the Glue architecture into its three named components. Start with the input sources on the left: S3, relational databases, a warehouse, DynamoDB, and SQL-compatible sources where supported. In the centre, the Glue Crawler scans data sources and infers table structure. The Glue Data Catalog stores the resulting schema and metadata. Glue ETL jobs can then read that metadata, perform transformations, and write prepared data to destinations such as curated S3 datasets, Redshift, or another supported location. Notice the trigger and schedule panel at the bottom. It allows workflows to run when a schedule arrives or when relevant events occur, rather than requiring manual execution every time. The point is that AWS Glue supports both metadata discovery and repeatable integration. If the data is already clean and the application only needs to query it, you may use the catalog without a large ETL job. If it needs transformations or format conversion, the ETL stage becomes important. Those are distinct decisions.

scenes.title: Glue Crawler and Data Catalog
scenes.narration: This slide zooms in on a common metadata-discovery path. On the far left, an Amazon S3 bucket stores CSV, JSON, or Parquet files. A Glue Crawler reads samples from the source and infers a schema. Follow the arrow into the Glue Data Catalog in the centre. It creates or updates metadata such as table names, column types, partition information, and source locations. Notice the important caption: the data files themselves stay in S3. The catalog is a metadata repository, not another object-storage bucket. On the right, Athena, EMR, and Redshift Spectrum are examples of engines that can use cataloged table definitions to query source data, subject to permissions and supported configurations. The three numbered steps at the bottom repeat the flow: scan the data, update metadata, and query using the catalog. Remember that crawl results may need review if source files have inconsistent types, missing headers, or schema changes.

scenes.title: Design S3 Partitions for Query Patterns
scenes.narration: Here we're looking at a subtle but important design choice: how object paths in S3 support efficient queries. The left panel shows sensor records partitioned primarily by date. That layout can be useful when the dominant question asks for all devices over a particular day or month. The right panel organizes the same kind of data by device identifier before date. That can be more suitable when queries normally focus on one device over time. Follow each query pattern to the highlighted S3 objects. A well-designed partition scheme lets the query engine skip many unrelated files, reducing scanned data and improving performance. But it does not guarantee that every query becomes faster. Extremely high-cardinality or tiny partitions can create their own overhead. Look at the takeaway along the bottom: storage layout should match your most common query filters. For an AWS exam question, first identify which column is filtered most often and how much data can be pruned, then evaluate the partition strategy.

scenes.title: AWS Glue Studio
scenes.narration: Glue Studio provides a visual way to build and monitor ETL workflows. Follow the three main columns across the slide. On the left are data sources, including S3 and supported streaming or JDBC sources. In the middle is a visual directed acyclic graph, or DAG, with nodes for sample data, transformations, and joins. This is where a developer defines how records are cleaned, enriched, and combined. On the right are output destinations: a curated S3 location or updated catalog metadata. Notice the example output folder layout organized by date partitions. The monitoring panel shows job execution status, duration, records processed, and resource-related metrics. It's important not to confuse a visual authoring tool with zero operational responsibility. Jobs still need correct permissions, sufficient processing resources, appropriate retries, and meaningful validation. The broader lesson is that a repeatable ETL graph can make data preparation easier to inspect and maintain than a series of undocumented manual steps.

scenes.title: AWS Glue Data Quality
scenes.narration: Now we add checks to the ETL workflow. On the far left, a developer authors or recommends rules using the Data Quality Definition Language, often abbreviated DQDL. Examples include completeness, uniqueness, and allowed ranges. In the next stage, a Glue job evaluates these rules against the dataset. Look at the result panel: each rule can pass or fail depending on whether the source records meet the expectation. The two branches on the right demonstrate different failure handling strategies. One branch stops or fails the job when quality requirements are critical. The other alerts or reports observations while allowing the workflow to continue. CloudWatch and other reporting surfaces can expose these results for investigation. The key point is that data-quality checks are deliberate application decisions. Choose whether a violation is fatal or reportable according to the downstream business risk. Good data quality upstream helps avoid misleading analytics and poorly grounded AI answers downstream.

scenes.title: Data Quality Check in Action
scenes.narration: This final slide turns the data-quality idea into a worked example. Begin with the customer order table at the top. The source contains duplicate order identifiers, a missing value, and an invalid amount. The lower flow sends raw CSV data from S3 into AWS Glue, where the records are transformed and then evaluated by Data Quality rules. On the right, the checks test completeness, uniqueness, and valid ranges. Notice that different rules have different results: some rows pass while others fail. The remediation loop beneath the flow sends failed records for investigation and repair before data is trusted downstream. The takeaway is that visual transformation alone isn't enough. We need measurable constraints on the fields the business relies on, and we need a documented response when those constraints are violated. This is especially important before feeding enterprise data into retrieval systems, analytics applications, or automated decisions. In the next lecture, we'll extend the pipeline with monitoring and operational diagnostics.
